name: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome
aliases: congenital absence of the uterus and vagina

reference.source: Speroff's Clinical Gynecologic Endocrinology and Infertility
clinicalPearls: MRKH is congenital aplasia of the uterus and the upper (proximal) two-thirds of the vagina resulting from müllerian (paramesonephric) duct agenesis in a phenotypically normal 46,XX woman with functioning ovaries.
It is the second most common cause of primary amenorrhoea after gonadal dysgenesis and typically presents in adolescence with primary amenorrhoea despite normal breast and pubic-hair development.

Because the ovaries develop independently of the müllerian ducts and function normally, secondary sexual characteristics, cyclical hormone production and ovulation are preserved, with normal gonadotrophins and oestradiol.
Examination shows normal external genitalia with a short, blind-ending vaginal dimple or pouch and an absent or rudimentary uterus.

Type 1 (typical, isolated) is symmetrical uterovaginal aplasia with normal fallopian tubes and no extragenital anomaly; Type 2 (atypical) and the MURCS association add renal, skeletal (vertebral, Klippel-Feil) and, less often, cardiac and auditory anomalies.
Renal tract anomalies such as unilateral renal agenesis and ectopic or horseshoe kidney occur in a substantial proportion, so upper urinary tract imaging is mandatory.
First-line creation of a functional vagina is non-surgical self-dilation (Frank technique); vaginoplasty (Vecchietti, McIndoe, Davydov or bowel) is reserved for those who fail or decline dilation.

Ovulation is intact, so genetic parenthood is achievable through oocyte retrieval with gestational surrogacy and, increasingly, uterus transplantation; functioning endometrium in a rudimentary horn can rarely cause cyclical pain and haematometra.
reference.pathophysiology: MRKH arises from failure of development of the müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts during embryogenesis, when these ducts would normally fuse and canalise to form the uterus, cervix and upper two-thirds of the vagina; the result is aplasia or hypoplasia of these structures, while the lower vagina, derived from the urogenital sinus, persists as a short pouch. Ovaries and fallopian tubes develop from separate lineages that are independent of the müllerian ducts, so ovarian endocrine and germ-cell function is retained and the karyotype is 46,XX with a normal female hormonal milieu. The aetiology is heterogeneous and largely sporadic, with familial clustering in some kindreds suggesting polygenic or multifactorial inheritance and implicating genes that govern müllerian duct and mesodermal development. The frequent coexistence of renal and skeletal anomalies reflects the shared intermediate-mesoderm origin of the urogenital and axial skeletal systems, which underlies the MURCS association.
additionalDifferentials: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY, absent or scant pubic hair, testes, absent uterus)
Isolated distal vaginal agenesis with an intact uterus
Cervical agenesis or dysgenesis with a functioning uterus
Gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Turner or Swyer syndrome)
Functional hypothalamic or constitutional causes of primary amenorrhoea with normal anatomy
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype to confirm 46,XX and exclude androgen insensitivity and gonadal dysgenesis
Pelvic ultrasound and, definitively, pelvic MRI to assess uterine remnants, functioning endometrium and vaginal length
Renal tract imaging (ultrasound and MR urogram) for associated anomalies
Serum FSH, LH and oestradiol (expected normal) and serum testosterone to distinguish androgen insensitivity
Spinal and skeletal imaging where vertebral or Klippel-Feil anomalies are suspected
Audiological assessment and echocardiography in atypical or MURCS presentations
Ovarian reserve assessment (antral follicle count and anti-müllerian hormone) if assisted reproduction is planned
redFlags: Cyclical or progressive pelvic pain from an obstructed functioning uterine remnant or haematometra requiring surgical excision
Undiagnosed renal anomaly such as a solitary or ectopic kidney affecting anaesthetic and surgical planning
Severe psychological distress, low mood or suicidal ideation following the diagnosis
Skeletal anomalies causing spinal deformity or, in MURCS, cardiac lesions needing evaluation
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and, with vaginal dilation or vaginoplasty, satisfactory sexual function is achievable for most women. Fertility requires assisted reproduction with surrogacy or uterus transplantation, and the long-term outcome is strongly influenced by psychological support around the diagnosis.
pitfalls: Confusing MRKH with complete androgen insensitivity, when pubic and axillary hair with a 46,XX karyotype distinguish MRKH and gonadal management differs entirely
Omitting renal tract imaging and missing a clinically important solitary or ectopic kidney
Overlooking a functioning rudimentary uterine horn as a treatable cause of cyclical pain
Proceeding to surgical vaginoplasty before offering first-line dilation therapy
Neglecting the profound psychological impact and failing to arrange specialist counselling and peer support
references: Speroff's Clinical Gynecologic Endocrinology and Infertility
ACOG Committee Opinion: Müllerian Agenesis — Diagnosis, Management, and Treatment
management: First-line graduated vaginal self-dilation (Frank technique) to create a functional neovagina
Surgical vaginoplasty (Vecchietti, McIndoe skin-graft or bowel vaginoplasty) reserved for those in whom dilation fails or is declined
Structured psychological support and peer counselling addressing diagnosis disclosure, body image and sexual identity
Fertility counselling offering assisted reproduction with the woman's own retrieved oocytes via gestational surrogacy, or uterus transplantation in selected centres
Mandatory upper urinary tract imaging with urology referral for associated renal anomalies, plus skeletal and cardiac assessment in atypical or MURCS forms
Multidisciplinary follow-up spanning gynaecology, adolescent medicine, urology and clinical psychology into adulthood
Genetic counselling for the family, acknowledging the usually sporadic occurrence with occasional familial clustering
